about: 인스타 sci(도파민 과학) 전용 추가 주제 — shorts_catalog.json(구미호 영어 쇼츠)의 survival·compare 항목과 같은 모양(n ≥ 901). 구미호 쇼츠에는 쓰지 않는다(두 채널 섞지 않기). pick_plan.sci_entry 가 shorts_catalog 다음으로 여기서 찾는다. 숫자는 facts 에만 · 출처는 기관·논문 원문에서 확인(2026-10-20).

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Inside a Tornado?

facts.fact: Tornadic wind speeds are generally believed to reach as high as 300 mph (about 480 km/h, converted) in the most violent tornadoes, enough to make automobiles airborne.
The strongest tornado wind measured by mobile Doppler radar above ground level was 318 mph (about 512 km/h, converted).
A typical tornado travels at around 10-20 mph (about 16-32 km/h, converted); movement ranges from almost stationary to more than 60 mph (about 97 km/h, converted).
The time a tornado stays on the ground ranges from an instant to several hours; the average is about 5 minutes.
The biggest threat to living creatures from tornadoes is flying debris and being tossed about in the wind; the old idea that low pressure makes buildings 'explode' is no longer believed to be true.
About 1,200 tornadoes hit the U.S. each year.
Engineers say many homes are rated to withstand winds to 100 mph (about 160 km/h, converted).
In a tornado warning, go to a basement, safe room or an interior room away from windows; sheds, mobile homes and tents are not safe.

beat_ideas.what: the wall of wind arrives: the most violent tornadoes reach about 480 km/h
the strongest wind ever measured by radar: 512 km/h
many houses are built for about 160 km/h: three times less
the danger is not the pressure but what flies in the wind (debris), cars can go airborne
an average tornado stays on the ground about 5 minutes
verdict line: the way to 'last' is a basement or an interior room away from windows

careful: No source gives a survival time inside a tornado: no clock, the verdict is the shelter rule (basement, interior room, away from windows)
300 mph is an estimate for the most violent tornadoes: say 'up to about'
Don't name real tornado events, dates or towns (real victims)
No injuries or bodies: say 'flying debris' and 'cars can fly', nothing more
km/h values are converted from mph: say 'about'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last at the Edge of a Lava Lake?
survival.situation: THE EDGE OF A LAVA LAKE

facts.fact: Lava erupts from Kilauea (Hawaii) at a temperature of 1,150 °C (2,100 °F).
Lava-lake crust counts as solid only below 850 °C (1,560 °F); between 850 and 1,070 °C it is semi-solid, and basalt can stay molten as low as 750-850 °C.
On April 1, 2021 the active part of the lava lake in Kilauea's Halemaumau crater was 224 m (735 ft) deep.
In the 1959 Kilauea Iki lava lake the crust kept breaking up: within seconds, or at most a minute, a major crack would form and blocks of crust slid under into the molten lava.
The 1959 Kilauea Iki eruption had 17 episodes of lava fountains in about 5 weeks.
During the 2022 lava-lake eruption, Kilauea's summit released about 1,900 tonnes of sulfur dioxide per day.
Sulfur dioxide is a colorless gas with a pungent odor that irritates the skin and the eyes, nose and throat; at Kilauea it makes volcanic smog (vog).

beat_ideas.what: the glowing lake in front of you: lava at 1,150 °C
it is deep: 224 m of molten rock in the active part (2021)
the dark crust looks like ground, but 'solid' still means under 850 °C
and it does not stay put: within seconds or a minute a big crack opens
the air: about 1,900 tonnes of sulfur dioxide a day, stinging eyes, nose and throat
verdict line: lava lakes are watched from a distance, from the crater rim

careful: Stand at the edge only: never describe falling in or a body burning (no gore)
No source gives a time for the heat at the edge: no clock
Lake depth and gas numbers are for a specific date (2021, 2022): say '그때'
No real people or accidents

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Inside a Giant-Hail Supercell?

facts.fact: Updrafts in a supercell can reach speeds of more than 100 mph (160 km/h), enough to support very large hail up to grapefruit size.
facts.evidence: Updrafts in supercell can attain speeds more than 100 mph (160 km/h). Such velocities are able to support the formation of very large hail up to size of grapefruit.

facts.fact: To hold up softball-size hail (4 1/2 inches, 11.4 cm), an updraft of about 103 mph (166 km/h) is needed.
The largest hailstone recovered in the United States had a diameter of 8 inches (about 20 cm, converted) and weighed 1 lb 15 oz (about 0.88 kg, converted).
facts.evidence: The largest hailstone recovered in the United States fell in Vivian, South Dakota, on June 23, 2010, with a diameter of 8 inches and a circumference of 18.62 inches. It weighed 1 lb 15 oz.

facts.fact: Hail falls when it becomes heavy enough to overcome the strength of the thunderstorm updraft and is pulled toward the earth by gravity.
facts.evidence: Hail falls when it becomes heavy enough to overcome the strength of the thunderstorm updraft and is pulled toward the earth by gravity.

facts.fact: In the strongest supercells, hailstones 2 to 4 inches across are expected to fall at 44 to 72 mph (about 71-116 km/h, converted).
facts.evidence: In the strongest supercells that produce some of the largest hail one might expect to see (2-inches to 4-inches in diameter), the expected fall speed is between 44 and 72 mph.

facts.fact: Very large hailstones, more than 4 inches across, can fall at over 100 mph (about 160 km/h, converted).
facts.evidence: However, it is possible for very large hailstones (diameters exceeding 4-inches) to fall at over 100 mph.

facts.fact: Some severe thunderstorms can produce hail larger than softballs or winds over 100 mph.
facts.evidence: Some severe thunderstorms can produce hail larger than softballs or winds over 100 mph

facts.fact: If severe thunderstorms are approaching while you are outside, go inside a sturdy building immediately; sheds and storage facilities are not safe.
facts.evidence: Go inside a sturdy building immediately if severe thunderstorms are approaching. Sheds and storage facilities are not safe.

beat_ideas.what: inside the storm the updraft blows upward at more than 160 km/h, holding ice in the air
a softball-size stone (11.4 cm) needs an updraft of about 166 km/h to stay up
the stone keeps growing until it is too heavy for the updraft, then gravity wins
the biggest stone found in the U.S.: about 20 cm across, about 0.88 kg
stones bigger than a softball can hit the ground at over 160 km/h
verdict line: no clock, the way to 'last' is getting inside a sturdy building, sheds are not safe

careful: No source gives a survival time inside a hail storm: no clock, the verdict is the shelter rule (sturdy building, not sheds)
Fall speeds are estimates with much uncertainty (shape, melting, orientation): say 'about' / 'can'
The 8-inch stone is the U.S. record (largest recovered in the United States), not a world record
Updraft speeds in the size table are approximate
km/h, cm and kg values marked 'converted' are converted: say 'about'
Don't name real storms, towns or dates; no injuries, just 'large hail is dangerous in the open'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Standing on a Comet?

facts.fact: Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko is so small that its gravitational pull is several hundred thousand times weaker than on Earth.
facts.evidence: Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko is so small that its gravitational pull is several hundred thousand times weaker than on Earth.

facts.fact: The comet has two lobes: the small lobe measures 2.6 x 2.3 x 1.8 km and the large lobe 4.1 x 3.3 x 1.8 km.
facts.evidence: the small lobe measures 2.6 × 2.3 × 1.8 km and the large lobe 4.1 × 3.3 × 1.8 km.

facts.fact: Rosetta's radio science instrument measured the comet's mass at 10 billion tonnes, giving a density of only 470 kg per cubic metre.
facts.evidence: the Radio Science Instrument has measured its mass to be 10 billion tonnes, yielding a density of 470 kg/m

facts.fact: The comet has a very high porosity of 70-80%: its inside is likely weakly bonded ice-dust clumps with small void spaces between them.
facts.evidence: the comet has a very high porosity of 70-80%, with the interior structure likely comprising weakly bonded ice-dust clumps with small void spaces between them.

facts.fact: Rosetta measured an average surface temperature of -70°C on the comet, which suggests the surface is mostly dust rather than ice.
facts.evidence: revealed an average surface temperature of -70°C. This implies the surface is predominantly covered in dust rather than ice, which would yield a lower temperature.

facts.fact: The 2.5-mile-wide (4-kilometer) comet was releasing the equivalent of 40 ounces (1.2 liters) of water into space every second at the end of August 2014.
facts.evidence: The 2.5-mile-wide (4-kilometer) comet was releasing the earthly equivalent of 40 ounces (1.2 liters) of water into space every second at the end of August 2014.

facts.fact: After its first touchdown, Rosetta's lander lifted off the surface again for 1 hour 50 minutes, travelling about 1 km at a speed of 38 cm/s (about 1.4 km/h, converted).
facts.evidence: the lander lifted from the surface again - for 1 hour 50 minutes. During that time, it travelled about 1 km at a speed of 38 cm/s.

beat_ideas.what: you land on a dusty, dark mountain only 4 km wide, drifting through space
the ground is cold: an average surface of -70°C
gravity is several hundred thousand times weaker than on Earth: you barely weigh anything
a 'touchdown' can turn into a 1 hour 50 minute hop: the lander floated about 1 km at 38 cm/s
the ground under your feet is 70-80% empty space, and the comet breathes out 1.2 liters of water every second
verdict line: with no air and almost no gravity, the only way to stay is anchored, in a sealed suit

careful: No source here gives an escape velocity or a survival time: no clock, say 'you could float away' only as an idea, not a number
-70°C is an average surface temperature from early Rosetta observations, before closest approach to the Sun: say '평균' and '그때'
Water rate (1.2 liters per second) is for the end of August 2014 and grew later: say '그때'
The lander hop is a spacecraft, not a person; do not name mission scientists
1.4 km/h is converted from 38 cm/s: say 'about'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last in the Path of a Pyroclastic Flow?
survival.situation: IN THE PATH OF A PYROCLASTIC FLOW

facts.fact: A pyroclastic flow is a hot (typically >800 °C), chaotic mixture of rock fragments, gas, and ash that travels rapidly away from a volcanic vent or collapsing flow front.
facts.evidence: a hot (typically >800 °C), chaotic mixture of rock fragments, gas, and ash that travels rapidly (tens of meters per second) away from a volcanic vent or collapsing flow front.

facts.fact: Pyroclastic flows carry rock fragments from ash to boulders across the ground at speeds typically greater than 80 km per hour (50 mph).
facts.evidence: rock fragments ranging in size from ash to boulders that travel across the ground at speeds typically greater than 80 km per hour (50 mph)

facts.fact: Pyroclastic flows typically move at speeds of over 60 miles per hour (100 kilometers/hour) and reach temperatures of over 800 degrees Fahrenheit (400 degrees Celsius).
facts.evidence: Pyroclastic flows typically move at speeds of over 60 miles per hour (100 kilometers/hour) and reach temperatures of over 800 degrees Fahrenheit (400 degrees Celsius).

facts.fact: Depending on the volume of material, the proportion of solids to gas, temperature and slope, pyroclastic flows can travel at velocities as great as 450 miles an hour (about 725 km/h, converted).
facts.evidence: Depending on the volume of material, proportion of solids to gas, temperature, and slope gradient, the flows can travel at velocities as great as 450 miles an hour.

facts.fact: The rocks and gas inside pyroclastic flows are generally between 200°C and 700°C (390-1300°F), hot enough to ignite fires and melt snow and ice.
facts.evidence: The extreme temperatures of rocks and gas inside pyroclastic flows, generally between 200°C and 700°C (390-1300°F), can ignite fires and melt snow and ice.

facts.fact: Even relatively small pyroclastic flows that move less than 5 km (3 mi) from a volcano can destroy buildings, forests, and farmland.
facts.evidence: Pyroclastic flows vary considerably in size and speed, but even relatively small flows that move less than 5 km (3 mi) from a volcano can destroy buildings, forests, and farmland.

facts.fact: Pyroclastic surges are ground-hugging clouds of ash, rock, and volcanic gas that move at hurricane velocities and have temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius.
facts.evidence: ground-hugging clouds of ash , rock, and volcanic gas that move at hurricane velocities and have temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius.

facts.fact: USGS advice: heed evacuation warnings if a volcano is known to be active.
facts.evidence: Heed evacuation warnings if a volcano is known to be active.

beat_ideas.what: a hot cloud of rock, gas and ash rushes down the slope, hugging the ground
its speed: typically more than 80 km/h, faster than any car on a mountain road
the fastest flows can reach about 725 km/h
inside: rock and gas generally 200 to 700°C, enough to start fires and melt snow
even a small flow, going less than 5 km, can flatten buildings and forests
verdict line: there is no clock to beat, the only way to 'last' is distance: leave when evacuation warnings come

careful: No survival time and no odds: the verdict is distance and evacuation, never 'you could outrun it'
USGS pages give different temperature figures (200-700°C for rocks and gas inside; over 400°C; typically >800 °C): say 'hundreds of degrees' or quote one range with its source wording
Speeds vary a lot: 'typically over 80 km/h'; 450 mph is an upper limit ('as great as'), and 725 km/h is converted: say 'about'
Don't name real eruptions, volcanoes or places with casualties; no burns or injuries described
Keep it neutral: buildings and forests, not people

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on the Surface of a Neutron Star?
survival.situation: ON THE SURFACE OF A NEUTRON STAR

facts.fact: A neutron star is the densest object astronomers can observe directly, crushing half a million times Earth's mass into a sphere about 12 miles (about 19 km, converted) across, similar in size to Manhattan Island.
facts.evidence: A neutron star is the densest object astronomers can observe directly, crushing half a million times Earth's mass into a sphere about 12 miles across, or similar in size to Manhattan Island

facts.fact: Neutron stars are so dense that a sugar-cube-sized piece of neutron star material would weigh as much as all of the people on Earth.
facts.evidence: Neutron stars are so dense that a sugar-cube-sized object of neutron star material would weigh as much as all of the people on Earth!

facts.fact: On the Cassiopeia A neutron star, the carbon atmosphere is only about 4 inches (about 10 cm, converted) thick, because it is compressed by a surface gravity 100 billion times stronger than on Earth.
facts.evidence: The researchers calculate that the carbon atmosphere is only about 4 inches thick, because it has been compressed by a surface gravity that is 100 billion times stronger than on Earth.

facts.fact: That thin atmosphere has a density similar to diamond and a pressure more than ten times that found at the center of the Earth.
facts.evidence: has a density similar to diamond and a pressure more than ten times that found at the center of the Earth.

facts.fact: The atmosphere's temperature is estimated to be almost two million degrees.
facts.evidence: The temperature is estimated to be almost two million degrees, much hotter than the Earth's atmosphere.

facts.fact: One pulsar (a spinning neutron star) spins 716 times per second (716 Hz), beating the previous record of 642 Hz; the fastest kitchen blenders reach 250-500 Hz.
facts.evidence: The newly-discovered pulsar is spinning 716 times per second, or at 716 Hertz (Hz), readily beating the previous record of 642 Hz from a pulsar discovered in 1982. For reference, the fastest speeds of common kitchen blenders are 250-500 Hz.

facts.fact: Magnetars, the most magnetic neutron stars, have fields of about 100 thousand million tesla, a thousand times more than an ordinary neutron star; Earth's field is some tens of a millionth of a tesla.
facts.evidence: Their magnetic field strength is about 100 thousand million tesla, a thousand times more than an 'ordinary' neutron star. By comparison, Earth's magnetic field strength is some tens of a millionth of a tesla.

facts.fact: Most data-storage media can be erased by a magnetic field of just one thousandth of a tesla.
facts.evidence: Most media used for data storage can be erased if they are exposed to a magnetic field of one thousandth of a tesla.

beat_ideas.what: a star squeezed into a city: half a million Earths of mass in a ball about 19 km across
one sugar cube of it weighs as much as every person on Earth
gravity 100 billion times Earth's: the whole atmosphere is squashed to about 10 cm
and that thin air is almost two million degrees
the ground can spin 716 times a second, faster than a blender at 500 Hz
verdict line: a magnetar's field is 100 thousand million tesla, when one thousandth of a tesla already wipes stored data: nothing made of atoms like ours holds together here

careful: Sizes differ by source and by star (about 12 to 14 miles): say '약' and 'a city-sized ball'
100 billion times gravity, 4 inches and two million degrees are for the Cassiopeia A neutron star: say '한 중성자별에서'
716 times per second is one pulsar (a record when announced, one of the fastest known), not every neutron star
The magnetar field is for magnetars, not ordinary neutron stars
No source gives a survival time: no clock; describe in neutral terms (squashed flat, not bodies)
19 km and 10 cm are converted: say 'about'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Off the Boardwalk in a Geyser Basin?
survival.situation: OFF THE BOARDWALK IN A GEYSER BASIN

facts.fact: The ground surrounding thermal features may look solid, but it can be just a thin crust with super-heated water below.
facts.evidence: The ground surrounding these features may look solid, but it can be just a thin crust with super-heated water below.

facts.fact: Yellowstone has more than 10,000 hydrothermal features.
facts.evidence: Great Fountain Geyser is one of more than 10,000 hydrothermal features in Yellowstone.

facts.fact: In Yellowstone the surface boiling point of water is 199°F (93°C), and the deepest circulating water of the hydrothermal system can exceed it.
facts.evidence: The deepest circulating water of the system can exceed the surface boiling point of water (199°F/93°C).

facts.fact: Steam vents (fumaroles) are often superheated, with temperatures as high as 280°F (138°C).
facts.evidence: Steam vents are often superheated, with temperatures as high as 280°F (138°C).

facts.fact: During an eruption of the park's best-known geyser, the water temperature at the vent has been measured at 204°F (95.6°C).
facts.evidence: During an eruption, the water temperature at the vent has been measured at 204°F (95.6C).

facts.fact: The highest temperature recorded in any Yellowstone geothermal area was 459°F (237°C), measured in a scientific drill hole just 1,087 feet (326 meters) below the surface.
facts.evidence: The highest temperature yet recorded in any geothermal area in Yellowstone was measured in a scientific drill hole at Norris: 459°F (237°C) just 1,087 feet (326 meters) below the surface!

facts.fact: Small hydrothermal explosions that create craters only a meter (a few feet) across or less probably happen annually to a few times per year.
facts.evidence: Small hydrothermal explosions that create craters only a meter (a few feet) across or less probably happen annually to a few times per year.

facts.fact: Always walk on boardwalks and designated trails in thermal areas, and don't touch thermal features or runoff.
facts.evidence: Always walk on boardwalks and designated trails. Keep children close and do not let them run on boardwalks. Don't touch thermal features or runoff

beat_ideas.what: one step off the boardwalk: the ground looks solid but can be a thin crust over super-heated water
around you: more than 10,000 hot springs, geysers, mudpots and steam vents
up here water boils at 93°C, and the deep water below goes past that
geyser water at the vent measured 95.6°C, steam vents up to 138°C
just 326 meters down, a drill hole measured 237°C
verdict line: no clock, the only way to 'last' is never leaving the boardwalk

careful: No survival time: the verdict is the rule (stay on boardwalks and trails), not a number of seconds
199°F/93°C is the boiling point at Yellowstone's elevation, not at sea level
Temperatures are measured values at specific features or a drill hole: say 'measured', 'up to'
The thin crust is 'can be', not every patch of ground
No burns or injuries described; don't name real visitors or incidents; don't tell viewers to go touch or test the water

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Inside a Desert Dust Storm?
survival.situation: CAUGHT INSIDE A DESERT DUST STORM

facts.fact: In a radar study of Arizona dust storms, the median dust storm depth was 5600 ft (about 1,700 m, converted).
facts.evidence: Median depth: 5600 ft.

facts.fact: In one large Arizona dust storm, Doppler radar showed widespread winds of more than 40 to 50 mph (60 to 80 km/h) as the dust cloud rolled forward.
facts.evidence: Doppler radar data indicated widespread winds in excess of 40 to 50 MPH (60 to 80 KPH) as the cloud rolled northwest.

facts.fact: Blinding, choking dust can cut visibility to near zero in just one to two minutes, which can lead to chain collisions on roads.
facts.evidence: Blinding, choking dust can reduce visibility to near zero in just one to two minutes, causing accidents that may involve chain collisions, creating massive pileups.

facts.fact: Dust storms usually last only 10 to 30 minutes, though dusty conditions may remain for some time afterward.
facts.evidence: Dust storms usually last only 10 to 30 minutes, though dusty conditions may remain for some time afterward.

facts.fact: A dust storm that hit Phoenix, Arizona in 2011 was a mile high (about 1.6 km, converted) and nearly 100 miles wide (about 160 km, converted).
facts.evidence: Just before 7:30 p.m. July 5, 2011, a mile-high, nearly 100-mile-wide dust storm roared through Phoenix, Arizona.

facts.fact: In that haboob, peak hourly PM10 dust levels at monitoring stations near Phoenix reached 1974 micrograms per cubic meter (and 907 for finer PM2.5 particles).
facts.evidence: This resulted in peak hourly PM 10 and PM 2.5 concentrations of 1974μgm -3 and 907μgm -3 at US EPA stations near Phoenix.

facts.fact: For comparison, the U.S. 24-hour air-quality standard for PM10 particles is 150 micrograms per cubic meter.
facts.evidence: PM 10 primary and secondary 24 hours 150 μg/m 3

facts.fact: If dense dust blows across or toward a road, pull the vehicle off the pavement as far as possible, stop, turn off the lights, set the emergency brake and take your foot off the brake pedal so the tail lights are not lit.
facts.evidence: If dense dust is observed blowing across or approaching a roadway, pull your vehicle off the pavement as far as possible, stop, turn off lights, set the emergency brake, take your foot off of the brake pedal to be sure the tail lights are not illuminated.

beat_ideas.what: a brown wall rolls across the desert: a typical dust storm is about 1,700 m tall
behind it, winds of 60 to 80 km/h push the dust forward
visibility falls to near zero in just one to two minutes: you cannot see the road
the air: peak dust reached 1974 micrograms per cubic meter, while the daily standard is 150
the good news: most dust storms pass in 10 to 30 minutes
verdict line: pull off the road, lights off, foot off the brake, and wait it out

careful: No source gives a survival time inside a dust storm: no clock, the verdict is the pull-over rule (off the pavement, lights off, foot off the brake)
5600 ft is a median from one radar study of Arizona storms, not every storm; 1,700 m and 1.6 km / 160 km are converted: say 'about'
60 to 80 km/h, 1974 micrograms and the mile-high size are from one large 2011 storm: say '한 번은' / '그때', do not present as typical

Do not name the storm's date or city on screen, and no crashes or injured people: say 'chain collisions are possible' at most

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last at the Geysers of Enceladus?

facts.fact: On Saturn's moon Enceladus, warm salt water, gases and minerals erupt through fractures in the miles-thick ice shell and blast through the surface at 800 miles (1,300 kilometers) per hour into space.
facts.evidence: Warm salt water, gases and minerals erupt through those fractures in the miles-thick ice shell and blast through the surface at 800 miles (1,300 kilometers) per hour into space.

facts.fact: Cassini has shown that more than 90 percent of the material in the plume is water vapor.
facts.evidence: Cassini has shown that more than 90 percent of the material in the plume is water vapor.

facts.fact: The ground around the tiger-stripe fractures is a numbing 50 kelvin (-370 °F) (about -223 °C, converted).
facts.evidence: they're a cozy oasis compared to the numbing 50 kelvin (-370 Fahrenheit) of their surroundings

facts.fact: Along one fracture, peak temperatures exceed 180 kelvin (minus 135 °F) and may be higher than 200 kelvin (minus 100 °F), warmed by the rising water vapor that drives the jets.
facts.evidence: peak temperatures along Baghdad Sulcus exceed 180 kelvin (minus 135 degrees Fahrenheit), and may be higher than 200 kelvin (minus 100 degrees Fahrenheit). These warm temperatures probably result from heating of the fracture flanks by the warm, upwelling water vapor that propels the ice-particle jets

facts.fact: Gravity measurements suggest an ocean about 6 miles (10 kilometers) deep beneath an ice shell about 19 to 25 miles (30 to 40 kilometers) thick.
facts.evidence: The gravity measurements suggest a large, possibly regional, ocean about 6 miles (10 kilometers) deep, beneath an ice shell about 19 to 25 miles (30 to 40 kilometers) thick.

facts.fact: Tiny silica grains in the plume suggest the ocean water was exposed to temperatures of at least 90 degrees Celsius, like hydrothermal vents on Earth's sea floor.
facts.evidence: if they were exposed to temperatures of at least 90 degrees Celsius

facts.fact: On its final close flyby in October 2015, Cassini flew through the plume at just 30 miles (49 kilometers) above the surface.
facts.evidence: Cassini flew through the plume at just 30 miles (49 kilometers) above the surface in October 2015

beat_ideas.what: you stand at a crack in the ice and it erupts: spray blasting out at 1,300 km/h
the ground around you is about -223 °C
the jet is more than 90 percent water vapor, freezing into ice grains as it flies into space
right at the crack it is 'warm': over 180 kelvin, still far below freezing
under your feet: 30 to 40 km of ice, then an ocean about 10 km deep
verdict line: the spray is watched from above, the way the spacecraft flew through it at 49 km

careful: Ice-shell and ocean depths are 2014 gravity-based estimates (and may vary by region): say '약'
-223 °C is converted from 50 kelvin: say 'about'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on a Beach When a Tsunami Arrives?
survival.situation: ON THE BEACH WHEN A TSUNAMI HITS

facts.fact: In the deep ocean, tsunamis can move as fast as a jet plane, over 500 mph (800 km/h), and can cross entire oceans in less than a day.
facts.evidence: In the deep ocean, tsunamis can move as fast as a jet plane, over 500 mph (800 km/h), and can cross entire oceans in less than a day.

facts.fact: Because its wavelength can be hundreds of miles, a tsunami is barely noticeable in the deep ocean and rarely more than three feet (one meter) high.
facts.evidence: Because of a tsunami's long wavelengths, which can be hundreds of miles, a tsunami is barely noticeable in the deep ocean and rarely more than three feet (one meter) high.

facts.fact: In 15,000 feet (4,600 meters) of water, a tsunami's speed works out to almost 475 mph (765 km/h).
facts.evidence: In 15,000 feet (4,600 meters) of water, this works out to almost 475 mph (765 km/h).

facts.fact: Entering shallow water near land, tsunamis slow to approximately 20 or 30 mph (about 32 to 48 km/h, converted), still faster than a person can run.
facts.evidence: As the waves enter shallow water near land, they slow to approximately 20 or 30 mph. That is still faster than a person can run.

facts.fact: Most tsunamis are less than 10 feet high (about 3 m, converted), but in extreme cases they can exceed 100 feet (about 30 m, converted).
facts.evidence: Most tsunamis are less than 10 feet high, but in extreme cases, can exceed 100 feet.

facts.fact: The time between tsunami waves ranges from five minutes to two hours, and the first wave to reach the shore may not be the largest.
facts.evidence: The time between waves ranges from five minutes to two hours. The first wave to reach the shore may not be the largest or the most damaging.

facts.fact: Just six inches (about 15 cm, converted) of fast-moving water can knock adults off their feet, and twelve inches (about 30 cm, converted) can carry away a small car.
facts.evidence: Just six inches of fast-moving water can knock adults off their feet, and twelve inches can carry away a small car.

facts.fact: If you are on the beach and feel an earthquake, no matter how big or how long, move quickly off the beach to high ground or inland, away from the water.
facts.evidence: If you are on the beach or near the water and feel an earthquake—no matter how big or how long it lasts—move quickly off the beach to high ground or inland (away from the water) as soon as you can do so safely.

beat_ideas.what: far out at sea the wave moves as fast as a jet plane: over 800 km/h
but out there it is rarely more than a meter high, ships barely notice it
near the beach it slows to about 32 to 48 km/h: still faster than you can run
most are under about 3 m, extreme ones over about 30 m
about 15 cm of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet
waves keep coming minutes to hours apart, and the first is not always the biggest
verdict line: no clock, the way to 'last' is leaving the beach for high ground or inland right away

careful: No survival time: the verdict is to move off the beach to high ground or inland, never 'you could outswim it'
Speeds depend on water depth: 'over 500 mph' and 'almost 475 mph in 15,000 feet' are examples, not one fixed speed
km/h, m and cm values marked 'converted' are converted from mph, feet and inches: say 'about'

Don't name real tsunamis, dates or places with casualties; no injuries described

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Caught in an Avalanche?

facts.fact: Slab avalanches can reach 60-80 mph (about 97-129 km/h, converted) within five seconds.
facts.evidence: Slab avalanches can reach 60-80 mph within five seconds.

facts.fact: Avalanches generally occur on slopes steeper than 30 degrees.
facts.evidence: avalanche generally occur on slopes steeper than 30 degrees

facts.fact: In 90 percent of avalanche incidents, the slide is triggered by the person caught or someone in their own party.
facts.evidence: In 90 percent of avalanche incidents, the snow slides are triggered by the victim or someone in the victim's party.

facts.fact: When avalanche snow stops in the runout zone it hardens quickly; even light, powdery dry snow can form concrete-like masses, and people are rarely able to dig themselves out of even very shallow burials.
facts.evidence: When avalanche material is deposited in the runout zone, it tends to harden quickly. Even very light avalanches of powdery, dry snow can form concrete-like masses after being "worked" by the mechanical forces involved in the slide.

facts.fact: Survival rates plummet after about 10 to 15 minutes under the snow, which is why each person carries a transceiver, a shovel and a probe and partners practise rescue.
facts.evidence: avalanche survival rates plummet after about 10 to 15 minutes

facts.fact: North American statistics suggest a completely buried person has a 50-percent chance of survival if rescued within 30 minutes, with a rapid decline after that.
facts.evidence: North American statistics suggest that a completely buried victim has a 50-percent chance of survival if rescued within 30 minutes, with a rapid decline thereafter.

facts.fact: A study of completely buried people in Austria and Switzerland found overall survival of 56%, with a second drop in survival to 25-28% at about 35 minutes of burial.
facts.evidence: Overall survival was 56% (Austria 59%; Switzerland 52%; p=0.065). The survival curves were similar and showed a rapid initial drop in survival probability and a second drop to 25-28% at ca. 35 min burial

facts.fact: People buried with an air pocket were more likely to survive, especially if buried for more than 15 minutes.
facts.evidence: Victims with an airpocket were more likely to survive, especially if buried >15 min.

beat_ideas.what: a slope steeper than 30 degrees cracks, and in five seconds the snow is moving 97-129 km/h
most slides (90 percent) are set off by the people on the slope themselves
when it stops, the snow sets hard like concrete: you can't dig yourself out
the clock: survival drops fast after about 10 to 15 minutes
an air pocket in front of the face buys time, especially past 15 minutes
verdict line: the real answer is prevention and partners: check the forecast, carry transceiver, shovel and probe, practise rescue

careful: Survival percentages come from different studies and regions (North America, Austria/Switzerland): say '한 연구에서'
60-80 mph is for slab (dry) avalanches; km/h is converted: say 'about'
No real accidents, places of accidents or people; no injuries, describe danger neutrally (buried, hard snow, little air)
Verdict is prevention and rescue gear (forecast, transceiver, shovel, probe), not a survival percentage
Do not tell viewers they can 'swim out' or dig themselves out: sources say this is rarely possible

compare.title_idea: Emperor Penguin vs Leatherback vs Cuvier's Beaked Whale | Deepest Dive Comparison

facts.fact: The deepest dive measured for an emperor penguin was 564 m; the longest emperor penguin dive lasted 21.8 minutes (a different dive and a different bird).
Below 1,000 meters no sunlight gets through at all (the aphotic zone).
The leatherback turtle's deepest recorded dive reached nearly 4,000 feet (about 1,200 meters, converted), deeper than any other turtle; it can stay down for up to 85 minutes.
Before 2014 the mammal dive records were 2,388 m and 120 minutes, both by southern elephant seals.
Tagged Cuvier's beaked whales dove to 2,992 m and stayed down 137.5 minutes, both new mammalian dive records (2014 study).
Their usual deep dives averaged 1,401 m and 67.4 minutes.

compare.twist_idea: CUVIER'S BEAKED WHALE held one breath for 137.5 minutes: over two hours in the dark.
careful: Depths are the deepest recorded dives, not usual ones (usual beaked-whale deep dive: 1,401 m)
1,200 m for the leatherback is converted from 'nearly 4,000 feet': say 'about'
'Sunlight ends' is not an animal: label it as the line where light stops
No people (free divers, submarines): animals only

compare.title_idea: Tortoise vs Bowhead Whale vs Greenland Shark vs Black Coral | Lifespan Comparison

facts.fact: Aldabra tortoises can reach sizes of up to 550 pounds (about 250 kg, converted) and ages of up to 150 years.
facts.evidence: Aldabra tortoises can reach sizes of up to 550 pounds and ages of up to 150 years old.

facts.fact: Stone harpoon tips recovered from bowhead whales show that bowheads live well over 100 years.
facts.evidence: Based on the recovery of stone harpoon tips from harvested bowheads, it is evident that bowhead whales live well over 100 years.

facts.fact: Newer age-estimation techniques suggest bowhead whales may live to be over 200 years old.
facts.evidence: However, new techniques allow for more precise estimation of bowhead whale age, and studies suggest they may live to be over 200 years old.

facts.fact: Scientists estimate the Greenland shark lives at least 250 years.
facts.evidence: Scientists estimate the Greenland shark lives at least 250 years

facts.fact: Carbon dating of proteins in the eyes put the largest Greenland shark studied, a 5-meter female, at between 272 and 512 years old.
facts.evidence: The largest shark they found, a 5-meter female, was between 272 and 512 years old according to their estimates.

facts.fact: The ocean quahog clam has a recorded maximum life span of 507 years, the longest-lived non-colonial animal known so far.
facts.evidence: with a recorded maximum life span of 507 years ( Butler et al. 2013 ), this species is the longest-lived noncolonial metazoan known so far.

facts.fact: Radiocarbon dating of deep-sea corals found the longest-lived gold coral (Gerardia) and black coral (Leiopathes) colonies were 2,742 years and 4,265 years old.

facts.fact: These deep-sea coral skeletons grow outward as slowly as 4 to 35 micrometers per year.
facts.evidence: show that radial growth rates are as low as 4 to 35 μm year

facts.fact: The living coral polyps are only a few years old, but they have been continuously replaced for centuries to millennia while building the colony's skeleton.
facts.evidence: Based on 14 C, the living polyps are only a few years old, or at least their carbon is, but they have been continuously replaced for centuries to millennia while accreting their underlying proteinaceous skeleton.

compare.twist_idea: The black coral colony is 4,265 years old, yet each living polyp is only a few years old: the colony keeps replacing them while its skeleton grows as slowly as 4 to 35 micrometers a year.
careful: All ages are estimates (radiocarbon, eye-lens dating, growth rings, harpoon tips), not birth records: say 'about' / '추정'
Greenland shark: 272 to 512 years is a wide estimate range for one shark; NOAA's general figure is 'at least 250 years': never say exactly 272 or '400 years'
Bowhead 'over 200 years' is what studies suggest, not a measured record
507 years is the maximum recorded for one individual clam, not a typical clam lifespan
The 4,265 and 2,742 figures are for coral colonies (many polyps over time), not one individual animal: label it 'colony'
150 years for the tortoise is an upper age, and 550 pounds is converted to about 250 kg: say 'about'
No people's ages or named individual animals on screen

compare.title_idea: Alaska vs Kamchatka vs Chile | Biggest Earthquake Magnitude Comparison

facts.fact: The San Andreas Fault is 800 miles long and only about 10-12 miles deep, so earthquakes larger than magnitude 8.3 there are extremely unlikely.
facts.evidence: The San Andreas Fault is 800 miles long and only about 10-12 miles deep, so that earthquakes larger than magnitude 8.3 are extremely unlikely.

facts.fact: Each whole-number step in magnitude means a tenfold increase in measured amplitude but 32 times more energy release.

facts.evidence: A magnitude 12 earthquake would require a fault larger than the earth itself.

careful: Sizes only: say nothing about casualties, damage or people affected
'Largest ever recorded' means recorded by seismic instruments (since about 1900), not the largest ever possible

1,600 km and 240 km are converted from miles: say 'about'
The San Andreas 8.3 fact is a USGS 'extremely unlikely' limit, not a real quake: never show it as one

facts.evidence: Approximately 6 million years ago, in what is now Argentina, an enormous bird ranged across the region from the Andes Mountains to the pampas.

facts.evidence: another pterosaur, Quetzalcoatlus , had a wingspan >50% greater than Argentavis , making Quetzalcoatlus the largest known flying creature.

facts.evidence: That top speed averages between 60 and 70 miles per hour (96 and 112 kilometer per hour) and can be maintained for only about 300 yards (274 meters).

facts.evidence: When it stoops--dives on prey--a peregrine may reach speeds of up to 200 mph.
